newsitem.title: USA: Florida officials "pleased" despite tobacco ruling.
newsitem.headline: Florida officials "pleased" despite tobacco ruling.

text.p: Florida officials said Tuesday they were not disappointed with a judge's ruling that stripped all but three counts from the state's closely watched 18-count tobacco lawsuit.
"We'll turn around and hit them somewhere else. We're still there and the trial is still set," Dexter Douglass, legal counsel to Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Douglass said Florida officials believed that Palm Beach County Circuit Judge Harold Cohen had left the most important parts of the suit intact in his ruling.
"Obviously we're pleased with the total result because the court has allowed us to go forward," Douglass said. The case is set to go to trial August 4, 1997.

Douglass also said he did not expect the state would have a problem complying with Cohen's order to identify sick smokers affected by the suit within 30 days. State officials said that information was computerized and readily available.

"The state cannot proceed without identifying each individual recipient of Medicaid payments," Cohen said in the eight-page order issued in West Palm Beach on Monday. He said the defendants must be supplied with the list of names -- which would number in the thousands -- so they can challenge any improper payments to individuals.

Cohen's ruling also barred Florida from seeking reimbursement for Medicaid payments made before July 1, 1994, when the law under which it filed its lawsuit was passed, citing a June Florida Supreme Court ruling on the law that said it needed modifications.
Cohen also dismissed three holding companies from the case -- Loews Corp, B.A.T Industries Plc and BATUS Holdings Inc, another B.A.T unit.
The judge did allow the state to claim the industry was negligent and made a dangerous product and ruled Florida can seek an injunction to prevent cigarette sales to minors.
"The major victory here is he upheld our right to seek an injunction to keep the tobacco people from enticing our children to smoke," Douglass said.
He also said the judge's ruling did nothing to prevent the state from amending its complaint to ask for punitive damages and that the state was considering doing so.
"It's still open to amend our complaint to ask for punitive damages... which our trial team is considering."
Florida is suing cigarette makers for Medicaid costs incurred by the state in treating tobacco-related illnesses.
